title: The United Monarchy Debate
lead: How large and how rich were the kingdoms of David and Solomon? The Bible describes an empire from the Euphrates to Egypt; archaeologists debate whether 10th-century Jerusalem was a capital of that kind or a small hill town, and who built the great gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer.

sections.b: Samuel and Kings describe a kingdom built by David and ruled by Solomon over all twelve tribes for about eighty years in the 10th century BC. David conquers Jerusalem, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom and Aram (2 Samuel 5; 2 Samuel 8). Solomon rules "from the River" to the border of Egypt, keeps a large court and thousands of horses, builds the temple and palace in Jerusalem, and fortifies Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer (1 Kings 4:21–28; 1 Kings 9:15–19). His ships trade with Ophir and his wealth draws the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10). After his death the northern tribes break away (1 Kings 12). Chronicles retells the same story with even more splendor.

sections.h: The gates of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer
sections.b: In the 1950s Yigael Yadin found a gate with six chambers and two towers at Hazor that matched one excavated earlier at Megiddo and a gateway at Gezer, previously misidentified. Reading 1 Kings 9:15, which names exactly these three cities, he dated all three to Solomon and took them as the work of one royal architect. For a generation this was the strongest archaeological support for the biblical kingdom. In the 1990s Israel Finkelstein proposed a "low chronology" that moves the pottery used to date these layers about eighty years later, making the gates the work of Omri's and Ahab's kingdom in the 9th century. Others answer that radiocarbon dates from Megiddo, Rehov and elsewhere allow a 10th-century date (Amihai Mazar's "modified conventional chronology"), that William Dever's excavation at Gezer supports Yadin, and that six-chambered gates are now known at later sites like Ashdod and Lachish, so the design need not be a single royal plan. The debate is still open.

The traditional view, held by scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen, takes the biblical picture as broadly historical: in a time when Egypt and Assyria were weak, a kingdom in the hills could dominate its neighbors for a few decades, and the lists of officials and districts look like real records. The minimalist or revisionist view, associated with the Copenhagen school and, in a milder form, with Finkelstein and Silberman, sees 10th-century Judah as a thinly settled chiefdom, with the first real state in the north under Omri, and the glory of Solomon as a later picture drawn in Josiah's time or after. A middle view, held by Mazar, Dever and many others, accepts a real but modest kingdom centered on Jerusalem, pointing to the Stepped Stone Structure, the Large Stone Structure, Khirbet Qeiyafa and the "House of David" in the Tel Dan inscription, while allowing that Kings has enlarged its size and wealth.
